claims.text: Controlled post-synthesis heat treatments can enhance short-range chemical order in high-entropy alloys without changing overall composition or inducing secondary phases.
The initial as-cast or thermomechanically processed alloy is a single-phase solid solution with minimal short-range order.
Progressively stronger annealing treatments will produce progressively greater short-range chemical order.
Increasing short-range chemical order changes the local atomic environment.
Ordered regions create enhanced barriers to dislocation propagation.
Short-range ordered regions impede dislocation motion more effectively than a random solid solution.
The increased resistance to dislocation motion caused by short-range order increases hardness.
The increased resistance to dislocation motion caused by short-range order increases yield and ultimate strength.
Annealed samples with higher short-range order will have measurably greater nanoindentation hardness than the untreated baseline.
Annealed samples with higher short-range order will have greater yield and ultimate tensile strength than the untreated baseline.
The proposed behavior is limited to annealing windows that preserve the primary single-phase structure and avoid precipitation, coarsening, and phase transformation.
Residual lattice distortion and other intrinsic microstructural features may alter the magnitude of the mechanical-property enhancement.
Compositional redistribution during annealing could make it difficult to isolate short-range-order strengthening from other strengthening mechanisms.
Electron diffraction or atom-probe tomography can provide a quantitative assessment of short-range order for the proposed comparison.

Failure of increased short-range order to produce a statistically significant increase in both hardness and strength, or observation of softening, would falsify the proposed governing role of short-range order.
